name: Undercut / fade with textured top

card.summary: A short-sided haircut with longer styled top, widely recommended for many face shapes; popularity is documented, attractiveness effects unstudied.
card.note: Claims of suiting many face shapes come from stylists and forums, not studies.

lead: The undercut with a fade and textured top is a men's haircut in which the sides and back are clipped very short, often tapering gradually to the skin, while the top stays long enough to style. People choose it to change the visible shape of the head and face: tight sides draw attention to the jaw, cheekbones and eyes, and volume on top adds apparent height and frames the forehead. A textured top means the longer hair is styled with product for body and a matte, tousled finish rather than a flat slick look.[1][5]

Wikipedia describes the undercut as a style in which the hair is shaved along a line above the ears, with the top left long and usually parted at the side or centre.[1] It dates to the early 1900s, was fashionable in the Jazz Age, faded in the 1960s, and returned in the late 1980s and again in the 2010s, when the top was often swept back with pomade or gel.[1] A fade is a tapered version of the short sides, in which clippers blend from shorter hair at the bottom to longer hair above; Wikipedia's haircut article lists 'fade' as another name for the short taper cut.[2] The combination popularised by the television series Peaky Blinders (from 2013) is widely discussed by barbers and in the press.[1][8]

No published study identified for this article has tested whether this specific cut changes how attractive someone is rated. A brand-commissioned photo survey led by Professor Marianne LaFrance, as reported by PsyBlog, found that different haircuts on the same man led raters to attribute different traits.[9] On looksmax.org, hairstyle is discussed as a quick, low-cost appearance change, with opinions on the undercut varying.[3]

paras: The undercut shaves or buzzes the back and sides and leaves longer hair on top; the line of the short section sits above the ears.[1] A fade creates a gradual taper on the sides, with the clippers arced out from the head as they move up.[2] Barbers build a regular haircut in a set order of edging (the lower hairline), siding (back and sides) and topping (crown and front), and clipper guards correspond to eighths of an inch, so a number 1 guard leaves about one eighth of an inch of hair.[2]

Modern barbershops usually describe the sides by where the fade starts (low, mid or high) and by how short it ends, with a skin or bald fade going down to the skin. The Wikipedia haircut article does not use those terms, listing only 'fade' as another name for the short taper, so the specific labels are barbershop vocabulary rather than an encyclopedic standard.[2] The 'textured top' is a styling choice rather than a cutting technique: the hair is usually cut to varied lengths and finished with a matte product so it sits in separated pieces.[5]

sections.h: How people use it to look better
paras: Short sides take bulk away from the sides of the head, so the face reads as longer and the jaw and cheekbones show more clearly. Contrast between the sides and a fuller top adds height, a reason people with thick hair or a wish to look taller choose it. Stylists and forum users also describe it as a way to shift attention away from the forehead or a rounder jaw. These recommendations by face shape are opinion from barbers and communities rather than research findings.[3]

The Wikipedia hairstyle article says healthy natural hair is regarded as an indicator of health, which it links to hairstyle's role in attraction, and that hairstyles also signal social class and group identity.[6] Wikipedia's undercut article notes the short-sided cuts were associated historically with working-class youth, while later versions were worn by celebrities such as David Beckham and Macklemore.[1]
Hair also interacts with other looks goals: people with thick hair, as in the looksmax.org thread below, often cite density as a reason to try the cut.[3]

Wikipedia lists the main types of styling product: gel stiffens hair into a set style, wax keeps hair pliable (the family includes pomade, putty and styling paste), pomade gives a slick look and can take several washes to remove, hairspray holds styles for long periods, and mousse is the lightest option, adding volume without the clumping of gel.[5] Clays and pastes are less strongly covered by the article.[5] The 2010s version of the undercut typically pairs the short sides with a gelled or pomaded top, while the textured version leans on matte wax or paste.[1][5]

Wikipedia notes that most products do not damage hair when used properly but can dry it out, and that some ingredients strip natural oils or build up, with scalp irritation including eczema and breakage or thinning reported; heat from dryers can also damage strands.[5]

Wikipedia associates the undercut with working-class youth and street gangs in the early 1900s, naming Glasgow's Neds, Manchester's Scuttlers and Birmingham's Peaky Blinders, and says short sides were thought to offer an advantage in street fights.[1] It became mainstream in the Jazz Age of the 1920s and 1930s; short back-and-sides cuts became the UK norm after World War I; and long-topped versions were popular among Wehrmacht soldiers.[1]

Short back and sides has much older roots: Wikipedia traces it to Roman legionaries, through the Renaissance and the Regency, and says it was the norm for professional men by about 1910.[2] The undercut remained common in the UK and US until the 1960s, when longer styles such as the wings haircut replaced it.[1]

The fade is commonly linked to military grooming in the 1940s and 1950s and to African-American barbershops and hip-hop culture from the 1980s, per a barbering-industry history; that page dates the military origin loosely and credits no single inventor.[7] Writers describe the barbershop as a place of community and ritual: one personal essay describes leaving the barber's chair with a stronger, more confident presence.[10]

In the late 1980s, centrally parted versions derived from the bowl cut appeared among new wave, synthpop and electronic music fans, and a collar-length 'curtained' style went mainstream in the early 1990s, worn by Tom Cruise among others.[1] The cut faded in the early 2000s and returned in the early 2010s among hipsters, skaters and punks, who often copied 1930s and 1940s versions with pomade and gelled tops; by 2014 it was fairly mainstream in the UK.[1]

sections.h: Peaky Blinders and the skin-fade era
paras: The BBC drama Peaky Blinders premiered on 12 September 2013, and its characters wear the short-sided, long-topped cut associated with the Birmingham gang.[8][11] LADbible reported in March 2026 that barbers described the screen cut as having no fade or blend and a side-parted mop on top, called it one of the UK's biggest haircut trends of the past decade, and quoted London barber TJ Hunt saying he did about ten of the cuts a week at the show's peak.[11] Many barbers pair the same shape with a fade, the combination this article covers.

The show's lead actor, Cillian Murphy, reportedly said he would not miss the haircut, calling it 'disgusting' and joking it should be called a 'lice cut', per the same report.[11] The Office for National Statistics separately attributed rising use of names such as Arthur and Ada to the show's characters, a measure of its broader cultural reach.[8]

Wikipedia reports that late-2010s press in the US and Israel linked the style to far-right figures such as Richard Spencer and Tommy Robinson, and that some neofascist supporters reportedly favoured it as a less severe alternative to the buzz cut. Nicknames such as 'Hitler Youth haircut' drew criticism from Jewish and progressive groups.[1] The article also notes that film and TV villains were often shown with undercuts in the late 2000s and early 2010s.[1]

No academic study of fades or undercuts specifically was found. Hair is discussed in the wider attractiveness literature. A survey led by Professor Marianne LaFrance, commissioned by a hair-care brand and summarised by PsyBlog, showed participants photos of the same people with different haircuts and found that hairstyles changed the traits observers attributed. For men, a short cut with a front-flip was rated the sexiest but was linked to being self-centred, medium-length side-parted hair looked more intelligent but more narrow-minded, and medium-length centre-parted hair had no effect on personality ratings.[9]
These are survey ratings of photos, not tests of an undercut with fade, and the survey was brand-sponsored.[9]

A looksmax.org thread asks whether a disconnected undercut is a good method for looksmaxxing; the original poster, who has thick hair, says many people including celebrities wear it and wants to see if it improves their look.[3] Replies were mixed: one said the style looks 'low class' unless worn by a footballer, actor or singer, while others treated it as ordinary.[3] Separate threads ask members to identify whether a given cut is a low or mid skin fade, showing the terminology in everyday community use.[12]
Hair is generally grouped with softmaxxing, the non-invasive end of looksmaxxing that Wikipedia describes as covering skincare, grooming, clothing and fitness.[13]

lore.intro: The undercut and fade are discussed on looksmax.org as an inexpensive way to change the shape of the head and face, with mixed opinions about the style.[3][12]

claims.claim: A disconnected undercut works as a looksmaxxing method
claims.believers: A poster with thick hair says the cut is worn by many celebrities and wants to try it to look better.[3]
claims.experts: No published study has tested the cut's effect on rated attractiveness. Wikipedia documents its history and popularity.[1]

claims.claim: Short sides make the jaw and face look sharper
claims.believers: Users and stylists say clipped sides expose the jawline and cheekbones.[3]
claims.experts: No research was found on perceived attractiveness of fades; a brand-commissioned photo survey found haircuts change the traits people attribute to the same man.[9]

claims.claim: Contrast between sides and top adds height
claims.believers: Proponents say the volume on top and tight sides make the head look taller.
claims.experts: No published studies have measured this effect.

claims.claim: The cut 'looks low class' unless the wearer is already attractive or famous
claims.believers: One forum reply says it looks low class unless you are a footballer, actor or singer.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia records the cut's history as working-class in the early 1900s and as a celebrity and hipster style in the 2010s; no study has tested class perceptions of it.[1]

claims.claim: Hairstyle changes the traits people attribute to a man
claims.believers: Stylists and hair brands say a haircut can change how confident or approachable someone seems.[9]
claims.experts: A brand-commissioned photo survey reported that different styles led raters to attribute different traits to the same man, though it is not a peer-reviewed trial.[9]

claims.claim: The Peaky Blinders cut is the template for the modern undercut
claims.believers: Barbers report heavy demand for the show's cut and variations on it.[11]
claims.experts: Wikipedia dates the undercut's revival to the early 2010s and attributes it to hipsters, skaters and celebrities, and notes the show premiered in 2013.[1][8]

claims.believers: Users treat pomade and wax as simple finishing steps.[5]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes products can dry hair, build up and irritate the scalp for some people.[5]

chain: Top left longer and textured for volume
Jaw and face look sharper and the head looks taller
angle.text: The cut changes the visible proportions of the head. Short sides narrow the silhouette and expose the jaw and temples, while a longer, textured top adds height and frames the forehead. It is a haircut, so the result appears immediately and grows out in weeks.
